prompt:
A single storyboard sheet from a 2D animated film, showing 4 wide 16:9 panels arranged in a clean 2x2 grid, all set in the same small cramped soviet-era kitchen in the morning. The four frames must feel like a continuous sequence from the same scene, with consistent character design, kitchen layout, colors, props, and lighting across all panels. The image should read like a painted storyboard page, not four unrelated illustrations.
Overall setting and style:
A small cramped soviet-era kitchen with lavender-grey walls #cfbad2, warm ochre floor #e8c088, morning light coming from the window side, pale lemon-yellow rim highlights on lit edges, cool lavender shadows, cheap worn domestic details, modest soviet atmosphere.
Style: dense opaque gouache, thick chalky matte pigment, dry-brush grain, wobbly asymmetric contours, flat matte color fields, hard-edged painted flat shadows, rough black ink scribble accents #060606 kept small in shadow creases. Imperfect, fast, hand-made, a painted storyboard frame aesthetic, 2D animation, not 3D.
Main characters, consistent in all panels:
The wife: tall, thin, stiff vertical figure, long narrow face, high forehead, long thin nose, tired half-lowered eyes with under-eye bags, small downturned mouth, deadpan expression as if everything is routine. Dark ink-navy hair #1c1230 with a middle part and a tiny topknot bun with a pale streak. Pale warm ochre skin #e8c088. Huge capable hands. Knee-length brick red-brown dress #784444 with a faint ring pattern, slouched light-grey socks #b2b2a2, navy-slate slides #2f3547.
The husband / dead man: lanky, stretched proportions, small narrow head on a long thin neck, huge hands, very long rope-like arms. In the “dead” state: acid chartreuse skin #9baf05 with olive shadows #7d9105, dark olive-brown messy hair and walrus mustache #514023, black X crosses for eyes, small wine-red tongue #7a1e46 sticking out, pale mint t-shirt #cdebd7 with deep forest-green stripes #1b4f2c, slim cropped dark aubergine trousers #23092b, cobalt slippers #22306e.
In the alive/blissful state: terracotta-orange skin #d4705a with red blush #c64842, short messy wine-red hair #78203a, wine-red walrus mustache #78203a lifted in a smile, eyes closed, white t-shirt with lavender tint #cfbad2 and thin navy stripes #1e2566, same dark aubergine trousers #23092b and cobalt slippers #22306e.
Panel 1 (top left): dragging him through the doorway
Camera inside the kitchen looking toward the open doorway in the lavender-grey wall. Through the doorway, framed by it, the tired middle-aged wife drags the dead husband backwards out of the dark corridor into the kitchen, holding him under the armpits. His limp body sags between her arms, his heels in cobalt slippers dragging along the floor. The corridor behind them is deep lavender shadow #4a3a52, with the front door far at its end. Warm morning light falls across the kitchen floor, while the doorway remains in softer shadow.
Panel 2 (top right): switching the plates at breakfast
Camera at table height, three-quarter view of the breakfast table by the window. Warm morning sunlight pours through the window with a thin cheap curtain. A red geranium sits on the sill, a ribbed radiator below. A small square table with faded floral oilcloth and two backless wooden stools. The dead lanky husband slumps sideways on his stool, head fallen back, long neck arched, black X eyes, tongue out, rope arms dangling to the floor. Standing over the table, the wife calmly swaps two plates of fried eggs without even looking at him, holding one plate in each huge hand, eyes half-lowered, expression deadpan, mid-routine.
Panel 3 (bottom left): embrace at the sink
Camera facing the back wall of the kitchen. Show the old cheap eighties kitchen set: dark warm wood-laminate #5a3532, peeling film at the corners, lower cabinets with worn countertop, an old white gas stove with a dented kettle, a white enamel sink with a tall rusty faucet and a thin stream of water running, a stack of clean plates beside it. Above are matching upper cabinets with dull glass doors, one hanging open on a crooked hinge. A frying pan hangs from a nail, a plain towel from a hook. At the sink, seen three-quarter from behind, the wife washes dishes, shoulders stiff, face in profile deadpan, one eyebrow slightly raised. Her husband is now alive and blissful, pressed against her back, his long rope arms wrapped twice around her, cheek against her temple, eyes closed, smiling.
Panel 4 (bottom right): theatrical corpse pose and her departure
Camera very low, almost at floor level, emphasizing the main depth axis of the kitchen. In the foreground on the warm ochre floor lies the lanky husband in an overacted theatrical death pose: back arched like a bridge, one hand pressed to his forehead, the other flung wide, one knee bent. He has acid chartreuse skin, messy dark olive-brown hair and walrus mustache, one eye a black X and the other cracked half-open, secretly watching, tongue slightly out. Beyond him in the middle distance is the open doorway in the lavender-grey wall, and deep through it in the dim lavender corridor the wife sits on a low stool by the front door pulling on street shoes, a suitcase beside her, her face calm and final. A thin sheet of water spreads across the kitchen floor from the sink side, its glossy edge creeping toward the corridor, catching small flat reflections. Warm morning light rakes across the floor.
Important composition rules:
Keep the kitchen layout consistent in all four panels so it clearly feels like the same place from different angles. Keep the wife’s silhouette rigid and vertical, and the husband’s silhouette elastic, floppy, and overlong. Preserve the contrast between her routine deadpan calm and his absurd corpse-like or theatrical physicality. The whole sheet must read as a coherent storyboard sequence from one animated film.

LOCATION
Small cramped kitchen: the square breakfast table with a faded floral oilcloth fills the lower foreground; at the back wall behind it, the old white gas stove with a black frying pan, dark wood-laminate cabinets around it and a white sink with a tall rusty faucet; warm window light enters from the right. FORMAT MODE
One continuous 8-second shot (oner), static locked camera, no cuts. The camera does not cut or move by itself. Diegetic sound only. 16:9, 24 fps.

OPTICS
MEDIUM-WIDE 29° from seated eye height at the table — both characters in frame at all times: the man large in the left foreground at the table, the wife smaller in the right background at the stove. Deep focus, everything sharp. No drift.

FIRST FRAME / BLOCKING
The man lies collapsed at the table in the left foreground (x ≈ 35%), torso slumped over the tabletop, right cheek flat on the oilcloth, face toward the camera, one arm hanging off the table edge — dead state: green skin, X eyes, tongue out. The wife stands at the stove in the right background (x ≈ 70%), back to the camera, stirring the pan with a spatula, weight on one leg.

ACTION TIMING
0.0–1.5s — hold: he lies motionless, dead; she stirs the pan, steam rises; the faucet drips slowly.
1.5–2.0s — his near eye cracks half-open: the black X unfolds into a narrow watching eye, the pupil slides toward her back. The rest of him stays limp.
2.0–3.5s — seeing her back turned, he slowly and carefully straightens up to sitting, long spine unrolling, rope arms lagging behind and settling late; as he rises, the color of life flows down him from the head: the chartreuse skin turns warm terracotta, the olive hair and mustache turn wine-red, the mint t-shirt turns white with navy stripes, the tongue slips back under the mustache, both eyes open round and content.
3.5–4.5s — he sits fully alive, satisfied, mustache lifted, hands settling on the table.
4.5–5.3s — at the stove she begins to turn: shoulder first, then head over her shoulder toward the table, spatula still in hand.
5.3–5.8s — the instant her head starts turning, he collapses straight back down like a dropped ragdoll: cheek hits the oilcloth with a dull thud, the arm flops off the table edge and swings, and a fast wave of green floods back over him from head to hands — chartreuse skin, olive mustache, X eyes, the tongue flopping out with a small overshoot.
5.8–8.0s — hold: he lies perfectly dead; her turn completes, she looks at him flat and unimpressed for a beat, then turns back to the pan and resumes stirring; the faucet keeps dripping.

PHYSICS
His body is a soft ragdoll: the rise is slow, the long arms trail and settle after the torso; the collapse is instant, full weight into the table — the tabletop shudders slightly, one plate gives a small clink, the hanging arm swings twice and stops. The tongue and mustache have follow-through. Steam from the pan drifts up steadily. Her turn carries weight: the hip shifts before the shoulders.

LIGHTING
Soft warm morning light from the window on the right: the lit side of his face and her back catch pale warm light, the room side falls into soft lavender shadow; the light lies on the table as one flat pale shape with a hard painted edge.

AUDIO
Diegetic only: the quiet sizzle of the pan, a slow steady drip from the faucet, a dull soft thud with one plate clink at 5.4s.

POSITIVE LOCKS
Static locked camera for the full 8 seconds. Both transformations happen in place, in full view, without cuts. By the time her eyes reach him, he is already fully green and motionless — she only ever sees him dead. The kitchen, the furniture and the clothes stay identical throughout. Clean crisp image.

CAUSE AND EFFECT — THE SPINE OF THE SHOT
Every move in this shot is an answer to the one before it. He pecks her → she gives him nothing, just puts the plate down → so he tries a real kiss and holds it → so she stops dead → so she has to get out of his arms → so he tries to hold her and fails → so she moves away, stands apart and leans away → then everything stops → then they look at each other → and only after that held look does he play dead. Nothing here happens on its own, and no two of these things ever overlap: each one finishes completely and the picture comes to a stop before the next begins.

HE IS PLAYING THE VICTIM
His collapse is not a breakdown and not a surprise — it is his next move, made after the affection failed. The order matters and must be visible: FIRST she finishes moving away and comes to a complete stop; THEN the picture holds still for a beat; THEN the two of them look at each other and hold it; and ONLY AFTER that held look does he begin to sag. It reads as a performance staged for her, and it needs an audience: her eyes are on him from the moment they meet his to the moment he lands.

HOW SHE GETS OUT OF HIS ARMS
His arms are a closed ring around her and she has to get out of it, and it has to be visible. She takes hold of his forearms and presses them down. HE RESISTS FIRST: for a beat his arms hold their shape against her hands and do not move, so the effort shows in her — her shoulders come up and back and her body works to lift itself out. Then his arms give and she is free. There is no violence in it, no jerk, no shove and no recoil, and she never once looks at him while she does it. She has done this a hundred times before and the pace is even and a little weary throughout.

THE PLATE
She is holding the white plate at the start of the shot. She lets it go down into the foam after the peck, and from that moment her hands are empty and stay empty. The plate stays in the basin for the rest of the shot and moves only for the one knock when he lands.

HOW SHE TAKES ALL OF IT
Nothing about her is startled or frightened at any point. She has watched him do this before and it shows in what she leaves out: no jump, no gasp, no widening of the eyes, no step back. When he falls, when the tap goes over and when the water rises she is the only thing in the frame that does not react.

THE WEIGHT OF HIS FALL
He is heavy and the picture has to say so. He gathers speed as he goes down instead of travelling at one even rate. He does not slow down before he lands and nothing catches him. He stops on a single frame and then holds without a tremor. What tells you how heavy he was is everything else on the counter moving at the moment he lands — the water leaping, the plates rattling, the drops jumping, the tap shuddering — while he himself lies there without moving at all.

She is behind the basin, facing camera, cut at the hips by the near rim of the sink, with the brass tap standing up in front of her body and her face clear above the curve of its spout. Her dark topknot is up, loose strands down her face, her brows raised, her eyes lowered, her brick red-brown dress. Both her arms hang down in front of her into the foam and she is holding a white plate.
THE HUSBAND STANDS IN THE RIGHT-HAND THIRD OF THE PICTURE. He is close behind her and to HER RIGHT, past the right-hand end of the basin, nearer to camera than she is. Her body covers most of him: what shows is his shoulder past her towards the right edge of the frame, and his head. HIS HEAD IS TIPPED LEFT TOWARDS HERS, temple against temple, and it OVERLAPS THE RIGHT-HAND EDGE of her topknot as a flat painted layer in front of it, the two heads touching with a clear painted edge between them and a strip of background nowhere between them. Both his forearms reach round her front and lie ON TOP of her dress, his hands resting on her with their digits held together.
The left-hand third of the picture, where the wire dish rack and the window curtain are, holds no figure at any point in the shot.

HE HOLDS ONE PLACE AND SHE IS THE ONE WHO TRAVELS

He plants himself in the right-hand third in the first frame and holds that exact horizontal place in every frame he appears in, right up to the frame where he leaves the bottom of the picture. Everything that travels across the picture is her.
She starts on his left and she ends on his right. She works out of his arms, travels once towards the right edge of the frame, passes behind the standing brass tap and passes him, and comes to rest out at the right-hand end against the bare lavender wall with clear wall showing past her. From that moment the two of them have changed places: he is the left-hand figure and she is the right-hand figure, and he did it by standing still.

BOTH OF THEM ARE FLAT CARDS FACING CAMERA

Both figures are seen front-on, square to camera, in every frame from the first to the last. Both of her eyes, both of her cheeks, both of her shoulders and the full front of her dress are visible in every frame, while she washes, while she works free, while she travels and after she stops. Both of his eyes and the full front of his striped t-shirt are visible in every frame. Each of them is a flat painted card held square to the lens, and all of their movement is that card sliding, lifting and tipping within the flat plane of the picture. They look at things by moving their pupils and their lids, as separate flat painted shapes sliding on fixed painted faces, while their heads and their bodies stay square to camera.

HOW HE GOES DOWN

He dies rigid and he falls rigid. From the moment the colour reaches him he holds his standing shape exactly as it is — arms, shoulders, chest, head, all of it keeping the same outline and the same distances they had while he was alive — and that whole stiff shape is what leaves the picture. He goes straight DOWN, keeping the same horizontal place across the screen, as one connected board with his head joined to his neck and his neck joined to his shoulders, everything travelling together at the same speed. The whole descent takes three exposed frames: he is standing, then he is halfway with his shoulders below the counter line and his head still above it, then he is gone. His shoulders pass below the edge first, his chin second, the crown of his head last. He is a felled plank going out of frame, and every part of him keeps its shape all the way.

HIS EYES ARE ON HER THE WHOLE TIME

His pupils sit low in his eyes and aim at her face from the very first frame, sitting towards the left side of his eyes to reach her. As she travels past him towards the right edge, his pupils travel across to the right side inside his eyes and stay aimed at her face, and they leave her only when the X marks replace them. His head holds one outline and one place throughout; the aim is carried entirely by the pupils and the lids.

HER EYES ARE ON HIM FROM THE MOMENT SHE STOPS

Once she has come to rest she turns her eyes on him and keeps them there. Her pupils travel to the left corner of her eyes, settle on his face across the room, and her lids come down a small way with them and hold. Her head stays square to camera and completely still while it happens, and her body stays square to camera and completely still. She holds that look through the colour, through the hold and through the whole fall, giving him nothing at all — flat, level and unimpressed, from a woman who has watched this a hundred times. Only once he is gone below the frame do her pupils travel downward, still on the left side of her eyes, to the floor below the bottom edge, and settle there.

HIS HANDS

Both his hands keep their digits held together in soft closed shapes for the whole shot, curled and relaxed, four digits to a hand.

THE DRIPPING TAP, AND WHAT THE DROPS ARE MADE OF

The brass tap drips from the first frame to the last, one drop every second and a half, evenly, and it keeps standing upright in the middle of the picture the whole time. The tap body itself stands completely still.
EVERY DROP IS A HAND-PAINTED GOUACHE SHAPE FROM THE SAME PAINT AS THE TWO FIGURES, laid on top of the room: one solid matte mid-blue tone across its whole body, flat, with a ragged dry-brush edge, a wobbly hand-drawn contour and visible paint grain, with a single separate flat white chip at its head. It belongs to the painted layer, in the same material as their skin and clothes.
The spout is turned away from camera, so each drop shows as a narrow painted mark falling just beside the standing column of the tap, down into the basin. Each drop is the same three stepped drawings, stepped on twos: a small matte mid-blue painted sliver stretches downward from the spout mouth, elongating like thick paint pulling away; it detaches with a snap, its tail whipping into a teardrop; it falls straight and fast as a short vertical brush-smear into the basin. The same size, the same tone, the same speed and the same path every cycle.
The foam already sitting in the basin keeps exactly the look it has in the reference plate and holds its place there.

TIMING

— BEAT ONE. He kisses her.
0.0 to 1.2 — the arrangement of the first frame holds. Her forearms move in the foam, turning the white plate over once, resting, and turning it again, and her shoulders move a little with the work. He stays exactly as he is in the right-hand third, his head against hers, watching her face. A painted drop falls.
1.2 to 2.5 — HE KISSES HER. One kiss, slow and long: his head pushes in towards her, his mouth reaches her cheek and STAYS there pressed against her, and his arms tighten around her waist as he leans into it. His place on the screen holds.
2.5 to 3.0 — SHE STOPS DEAD. Everything about her comes to a halt and her shoulders come up. She lets the white plate go: her hands open and it settles down into the foam, and her wet hands come up out of the water and rest empty on the rim. The stillness is what reads.

— BEAT TWO. She works herself free, and they change places.
3.0 to 5.2 — SHE GETS OUT OF HIS ARMS, AND THE WORK OF IT IS THE ACTING. First she shrugs the shoulder his head is resting on, one short sharp lift, and his head comes up off it. Then her hands come off the rim and take hold of his two forearms and press them down and away from her waist. FOR A MOMENT HE HOLDS — his arms resist under her hands and keep their shape, and she has to press harder, lift her shoulders up and back and work her whole shape upward out of the ring of them. Her lids come down once, all the way, and open again — one slow weary blink in the middle of the effort. Then his arms give and she is out. His arms are left open in the air where she left them and his mouth is left pressing on empty air. She stays square to camera through all of it.
5.2 to 6.6 — she travels TOWARDS THE RIGHT EDGE OF THE FRAME, past him, at an even unhurried pace, sliding sideways as a flat front-facing card and passing BEHIND the standing brass tap on her way, and comes to rest out at the right-hand end against the bare lavender wall, her whole shape well inside the frame. Her arms come down at her sides. HE HOLDS HIS ONE PLACE.
6.6 to 7.0 — she settles: her raised shoulders come down and her arms hang at her sides. She stands square to camera, facing us, and stops. HER BODY HOLDS STILL FROM HERE TO THE LAST FRAME.
7.0 to 7.6 — A FULL STOP. The whole picture holds completely still, with the brass tap standing alone in the clear middle of the picture between the two of them. A painted drop falls.

— BEAT THREE. They look at each other.
7.6 to 8.2 — SHE TURNS HER EYES ON HIM. Her pupils travel to the left corner of her eyes, settle on his face across the room, and her lids come down a small way and hold. Her head holds still and her body holds still.
8.2 to 9.6 — THEY HOLD THE LOOK. He stands on his place with his arms still open in the air where she left them, his pupils travelled across to reach her. Two flat painted faces, both square to camera, their eyes crossing the room between them. Neither of them moves anything else at all. A painted drop falls in the middle of it.

— BEAT FOUR. He dies standing and drops out of the picture like a plank.
9.6 to 10.4 — THE COLOUR GOES THROUGH HIM IN ONE WAVE running downward, from the crown of his head to the hem of his t-shirt: his skin turns chartreuse green, his hair turns olive, the navy stripes on his t-shirt turn green, all of it changing as the wave passes and staying changed behind it. As the wave crosses his face his pupils are replaced by two black X marks and a small wine-red tongue drops out of his mouth. HE STAYS STANDING UPRIGHT AND ABSOLUTELY RIGID while it passes, holding the exact shape and the exact pose he had a second earlier, arms still open in the air. Only the colour travels across the figure he already is. Her eyes stay on him.
10.4 to 11.0 — held. He stands there green, upright, stiff and completely still, arms still open. She is looking straight at it and giving him nothing.
11.0 to 11.1 — ONE FRAME OF LIFT. His whole rigid shape rises a hair on the spot, everything about him keeping its shape, and holds.
11.1 to 11.35 — HE DROPS OUT OF THE PICTURE IN THREE EXPOSED FRAMES. Standing, then halfway with his shoulders below the counter line and his head still above it, then gone below the bottom edge. He keeps his standing shape exactly through all three, arms open, head joined to his neck, everything travelling together at the same speed, straight down, on the same horizontal place. Her eyes stay on him as he goes.
11.35 to 11.9 — THE ROOM ANSWERS THE THUD FROM BELOW THE FRAME: flat painted blue shapes leap up out of the basin and fall back, the white plate knocks against the ceramic, the white plates in the wire rack rattle in place and one of them jumps, loose painted drops jump off the rim and fall, and the brass tap shudders once on its seat and keeps standing upright. She is the one thing in the frame that carries on as it was.
11.9 to 12.6 — the place where he stood is empty and her eyes are still aimed at it. The tap stands and drips, the rack settles, the foam settles back as it was. A held beat with the picture still. A painted drop falls.

— BEAT FIVE. Her eyes follow him down.
12.6 to 13.4 — her pupils travel DOWNWARD inside her eyes, staying on the left side, past the edge of the counter to the floor below the frame where he went, and settle there. Her lids come down a small way with them. Her head stays square to camera and completely still.
13.4 to 15.0 — held. She stands at the right-hand end against the bare lavender wall, facing camera, both eyes visible, looking down and towards the left, her lids open and still. The brass tap stands upright in the middle of the empty picture and goes on dripping in the same rhythm, one painted drop falling in the middle of this held stretch, and everything else in the frame holds completely still to the last frame.

CAUSE AND EFFECT — THE SPINE OF THE SHOT

Every move in this shot is an answer to the one before it. He kisses her › so she shrugs his head off her shoulder, works his arms down and off her, travels past him to the right-hand end and stops › everything stops › so she turns her eyes on him › so he looks back and they hold it › so he plays dead for her, goes green standing and drops out of the bottom of the picture › and her eyes follow him down. Each one finishes completely and the picture comes to a stop before the next begins.

HE IS PLAYING THE VICTIM AND SHE IS THE AUDIENCE

His death is his next move, made after the affection failed, and it is staged for her. The order matters and must be visible: FIRST she finishes travelling and stops; THEN the picture holds still for a beat; THEN her eyes come round onto him; THEN he looks back and they hold it; and ONLY AFTER that held look does the colour start. He needs an audience and he has one — her eyes are on him from the moment they find him to the moment he drops out of the frame. The joke is what she gives him for it, which is nothing at all: the same level look through the colour, through the hold and through the fall.

HOW SHE GETS OUT OF HIS ARMS

His arms are a closed ring around her and she has to get out of it, and it has to be visible. The shoulder shrug comes first and gets his head up off her; the hands come second and press his forearms down. HE RESISTS FIRST: for a beat his arms hold their shape against her hands, so the effort shows in her — her shoulders come up and back and her body works to lift itself out. Then his arms give and she is free. The whole thing stays even, weary and unhurried, and her eyes stay down on the water while she does it.

THE PLATE

She is holding the white plate at the start of the shot. She lets it go down into the foam when she stops, and from that moment her hands are empty and stay empty. The plate rests in the basin for the rest of the shot and moves only for the one knock when he lands below the frame.

HOW SHE TAKES ALL OF IT

She stays even and level from the first frame to the last. She has watched him do this before, and it shows: her stance holds, her lids hold, her mouth holds, and her pace stays exactly the same through the look, through the colour, through the drop and through the knock. She is the one thing in the frame that carries on as it was.

THE WEIGHT OF HIS FALL

He is heavy and the picture has to say so, and it says so with speed and with stiffness rather than with softening. He holds absolutely rigid, lifts a hair, and then goes in three frames without slowing anywhere. What tells you how heavy he was is everything else moving a beat after he is gone — the water leaping, the plate knocking, the plates rattling in the rack, the drops jumping, the tap shuddering on its seat — while the frame he left stands empty and still.

LAYER ORDER

Nearest to camera: the brass tap, the near rim of the sink, and the wire dish rack at the left-hand end, all passing IN FRONT of both figures as clean flat 2D layer overlaps. Then the painted drops, laid on top of the room. Then the husband, who is nearer to camera than the wife: his head, his shoulder and his forearms are foreground painted layers, his head overlapping IN FRONT of the right-hand contour of her hair and topknot and his forearms overlapping IN FRONT of her waist. Then the wife, who passes BEHIND the tap on her way across. Everything else in the room is furthest away and stays behind both of them. Her face and her topknot stay fully visible at every moment. His head stays a separate painted shape beside hers with a clear painted edge between them, and the two heads stay two shapes throughout.

RIGID PARTS

Her body is one flat painted shape facing camera and holds the same outline and the same size on screen for the whole shot; her shrug, her getting free and her travel across the picture are that same shape lifting and sliding in the plane of the picture, front-on the whole way. His head is one flat painted shape and holds the same outline and the same size on screen throughout; while the colour passes through him his outline holds exactly as it was, and while he drops his whole figure keeps every proportion and every distance it had while standing. HIS HEAD IS ATTACHED TO HIS NECK AND HIS NECK TO HIS SHOULDERS IN EVERY FRAME, one connected painted shape, keeping its own size and its own outline for the whole descent. Their upper arms, forearms and hands stay flat painted shapes turning at the shoulder, the elbow and the wrist, each keeping its length, its width, its colour and its painted texture, and each hand keeps FOUR digits throughout, held together in soft closed shapes. Both figures keep the same size on screen and the same size against each other for the whole shot, at the same depth from camera, and depth is never simulated by scaling either of them. All of their movement stays in the flat plane of the picture. Neither head ever rotates around the vertical axis, and neither figure is ever seen in profile or in three-quarter view. Their painted shadows are permanent graphic shapes attached to the artwork and stay identical.

STILL

The room is a completely fixed rendered background and every object in it holds the exact place, the exact size and the exact shape it has in the reference plate, from the first frame to the last. Nothing is added to the room and nothing is taken out of it. The sink holds its place and its shape, and the brass tap holds its place and stands upright to the last frame. The camera holds one fixed position, with no zoom, no pan, no tilt and no reframing, and the framing at the last frame matches the first.

MOTION LANGUAGE

Man kisses his wife over her right shoulder, so she shrugs his head off, works his arms down off her, slides across the picture past him to the right-hand end and stops, and the two of them have changed places. Everything stops. She turns her eyes on him, he looks back, and they hold it. So he plays dead for her: the colour goes out of him while he stands, he holds rigid, and he drops straight out of the bottom of the frame like a felled plank. Her eyes follow him down. The tap goes on dripping. Stepped limited 2D animation on twos, 12 frames per second, pose-to-pose, long held poses and few drawings between them. The painted characters move like articulated hand-painted animation cels over a fixed 3D rendered background, economical, graphic and readable.

The dragging forearm crosses in front of her dress, and the elbow stays tucked against the dress silhouette.
Where an elbow does come into view, the rounded end of the upper arm lies on top of the forearm and its contour stays visible crossing the shape beneath it; the arm turns at that overlap.
Each plate stays a rigid flat painted disc, level all the way, and its food is fixed to it and rides with it: the flat spread yellow on one, the ONE ROUND WHOLE YELLOW DOME on the other, the same round dome at the last frame as at the first.

7.2–8.0s: held. She blinks once more and holds to the last frame.

Her eyes stay level and forward on the far wall the whole way, away from the table and away from the plates. Her head keeps facing the camera and she stays seated exactly where she is. The pool is redrawn a few times across the shot, and each redraw is A BIGGER PIECE OF BLUE PAPER THAN THE ONE BEFORE, covering more of the floor.
Each of those shapes is HELD STILL on screen for a stretch of time, and then the next, larger one replaces it in a single step. Between one shape and the next nothing is drawn: the edge does not travel, it is simply somewhere further out on the next held drawing.
Each new shape CONTAINS THE WHOLE OF THE ONE BEFORE IT: the floor that was blue stays blue, and only the outline reaches further.
The shapes in order cover: the boards at the foot of the cabinet; then out across the herringbone parquet; then round the yellow bucket, closing on both sides so the bucket stands in the blue; then up to the big blue slipper on his straight leg; then around both his slippers and along the hem of his trousers, with white flecks where the blue meets his painted shapes.

The fountain plays at exactly the same height and the same width in the last frame as in the first: as much comes in at the end as at the beginning.

He holds the exact drawing he has in the first frame, from the first frame to the last: the same lopsided arrangement, the same limbs in the same places, the same flat chartreuse green skin, olive hair and moustache, the two black X marks, the wine-red tongue hanging out sideways, the half-off slipper hanging on his toes. THE LEAK — FOUR POINTS, EACH WITH ITS OWN CHARACTER
Water is getting through from somewhere above. WHERE IT COMES FROM STAYS OUT OF THE PICTURE: the drops enter over the top edge of the frame and nothing above that edge is ever shown or explained.
THERE ARE EXACTLY FOUR POINTS LEAKING BY THE END OF THIS SHOT, AND FOUR ONLY. They start one at a time, in this order, and EVERY POINT GOES ON DRIPPING FOR THE REST OF THE SHOT ONCE IT HAS STARTED. None of them ever stops.
POINT ONE, over the counter beside her: a slow one. A long wait, then one drop, then a long wait again. It is the loneliest of the four and it never speeds up.
POINT TWO, over the parquet in front of her, well to one side: an irregular one. Two drops close together, then a long gap, then one, then another two. It never falls into a rhythm.
POINT THREE, over the hob: a quick nervous one. Small drops arriving in little bursts of three or four, then a pause, then another burst.
POINT FOUR, right above her, over her shoulder: a heavy slow one, the slowest of the lot, with a long swell before each drop lets go.
THE FOUR ARE NEVER IN STEP WITH EACH OTHER. Their drops never land together and never settle into an even patter: at any moment one is falling, another is halfway down and two are waiting. What the audience should hear and see is four separate irregular rhythms overlapping, not a shower.
Between the four points the picture is empty: nothing falls anywhere else in the frame.
Each drop falls in three or four held positions on its way down.

HOW THE WATER IS MADE
The water belongs to the room and not to the painted woman: it is part of the same stylized CGI cartoon render as the stove and the counter, and it takes the same light they do.
ITS COLOUR IS A LIGHT BLUE-TEAL, about #8db9c9 where the light falls on it, going to about #588396 where it lies in shade.
EACH FALLING DROP IS TINY AND IT IS DRAWN AS A TINY THING: a small speck of that blue-teal, plain and even all over, with no detail on it at all, because at this size there is no room for any. It is a fleck, and it reads as a fleck.
ITS SIZE, BECAUSE IT MATTERS MOST: as wide as the dark grout line between two wall tiles, and no wider. About twenty of them would fit side by side across one wall tile. Held against a tomato on the counter it would be a pinprick on it. Held against her hand, a dozen of them would sit in her palm. Every drop is that same size from the first to the last.
The only place the water is drawn any larger is IN THE WET MARKS IT LEAVES: those are small flat rounded patches on whatever it lands on, each about as wide as one of the little metal lids on the spice jars, and they stay and gather. Those marks are what the audience actually reads.

WHAT HAPPENS
First: she cooks and wiggles through her three body drawings in that uneven order, easy and pleased with herself, HEAD A towards us, one hand stirring and one on her hip.
Then: POINT ONE LETS GO. A single drop comes down onto the counter beside her and leaves a wet mark. She stops dead on whichever body drawing she is in and holds it, her stirring hand stopping over the pan. Her head is still HEAD A.
Then: HER HEAD CHANGES TO B on one frame — she is looking down and out at the wet mark, eye wide, brow up. SHE HOLDS THAT, PERFECTLY STILL, FOR A LONG BEAT. Point one drips again once in that time and nothing else happens.
Then: POINT TWO STARTS, out to one side on the parquet, in its own uneven rhythm. Point one carries on. She holds HEAD B, still looking at the counter, while the second one goes on behind her.
Then: POINT THREE STARTS over the hob, in bursts. Now three points are going at once, out of step with each other.
Then: HER HEAD CHANGES TO C on one frame — chin up, nose past the top edge, eye round and pupil small. Her free hand comes off her hip and up in front of her, palm turned upward, the way somebody checks whether it is raining. Her shoulders and hips do not move at all. SHE HOLDS THAT, PERFECTLY STILL, FOR A LONG BEAT.
Then: POINT FOUR STARTS directly above her, and its first heavy drop lands on her shoulder and darkens the towel. She does not flinch and she does not move: she stays on HEAD C with her palm out.
Finally: all four points are going, each on its own rhythm, and she holds that pose to the last frame, looking up, palm out, her body still turned away from us and her stirring hand still resting where it stopped over the pan.

SHE IS A PAINTING ON GLASS
She is a flat painted image lying on glass in front of the room: an outline and a fill, with no thickness and no volume. Each frame of her is an individually painted drawing, and the shot reads as a chain of separate drawings rather than one model being deformed — her construction and her proportions stay identical from drawing to drawing. Her raspberry gown, her skin and her curlers keep their own flat painted colour whatever the room does around them, and she stays outside the room's lighting entirely: no shine, no reflection, no shading from the room falls on her. All of her movement stays inside the flat plane of the picture. Each hand keeps four digits held together.

WHAT HOLDS
Every object of the kitchen stays exactly where the first image has it, at the same size and shape, from the first frame to the last. The room holds exactly the plate's tone — the same lightness, the same gentle contrast, one calm warm look edge to edge, warm daylight from the window on the right and all shadows falling to the left. The camera holds one fixed position throughout, with no zoom, no pan and no reframing. Her size on screen never changes, and her outline, gown, curlers, towel, slippers and painted surface stay exactly as the second image has them in every frame. Her shoulders and hips stay turned away from the camera from the first frame to the last, and her head is only ever drawing A, B or C, each held still. Four leaking points and no more; each one keeps dripping once it has started; the drops keep one size throughout.

HOW IT MOVES
Limited 2D animation on twos: strong readable held poses replaced in single steps, with very few drawings between them. Between changes each pose sits completely still, and the beats after each head change are the longest holds in the shot. The drops move smoothly and continuously, each point on its own timing.

SOUND
A small radio playing off frame — cheerful tinny pop, a bit muffled, the kind that plays in a kitchen all day. Under it a pan sizzling. Then one soft tap alone, a long pause, another. Then a second rhythm joins somewhere else, then a third in little bursts, then a fourth, heavy and slow — four separate irregular tickings overlapping and never falling into step.
